places.rationale: A rich, well-governed, low-climate-risk country where modest growth easily clears the 'better' bar; the main drags are fast aging, very low fertility and 56% energy imports, and abundance needs a 5x jump that only superintelligence makes plausible.

Top-tier institutions, low debt, capital and pharma/finance strength make Switzerland one of the most resilient places and well placed to capture superintelligence gains; aging and Alpine glacier loss are the main slow risks.

Belarus has decent basic services but an authoritarian, Russia-dependent economy (71% energy imports) sitting on the Russia-NATO fault line, so war and political rupture are the dominant risks; ordinary convergence makes 'better' the most likely outcome.

From a very low base (living standard 7, 25% undernourished, 39% electricity) a 25% gain by 2100 is a low bar, but long-run stagnation, high climate vulnerability and weak readiness keep collapse risk among the highest; abundance would need a roughly 70-fold rise.

Togo is slightly ahead of its poorest neighbours on electricity and food and has a port-led economy, but weak political stability, a heavy interest burden and Sahel jihadist spillover into the north are real downside risks.

Hydropower exports, near-universal electricity and links to China's growth make sustained gains likely, though the debt overhang (89% of GDP) and weak government effectiveness can stall it and Mekong climate change adds risk.

A closed autocracy living off gas exports that the energy transition will shrink, with severe water stress (3.7) that depends on the Amu Darya and worsening heat; gas income still makes moderate gains the base case.

Hong Kong is very rich already (index 131), so 'better' needs real growth against the world's lowest fertility, rapid aging, eroding autonomy and full exposure to any US-China or Taiwan conflict; superintelligence led from China could still lift it a lot.

A divided, oil-dependent state (political stability -1.84) facing near-maximum water stress on depleting fossil aquifers and falling oil rents over the century, so collapse is a serious risk; reunification and solar desalination are the upside.

Low debt, universal electricity and hydropower potential support steady gains from a living standard of 23, but heavy reliance on Russian remittances, repeated political upheaval and glacier-fed water that shrinks later in the century cap the outlook.

A large food surplus, abundant clean hydropower and almost no water stress make Paraguay unusually resilient to global shocks; mediocre institutions, crime and droughts on its river trade routes are the main limits.

The entrenched dictatorship, mass emigration, 17% undernourishment and exposure to hurricanes and the Dry Corridor weigh against it, though a low base and low debt leave modest gains the likeliest path.

Convergence toward the EU should lift a living standard of 47, but steep population loss and aging, a coal-heavy energy system, democratic backsliding and Kosovo tensions add stagnation and conflict risk.

An oil-dependent petro-state with debt near 100% of GDP, very weak government effectiveness and 25% undernourishment; the energy transition threatens its main income, while ample water and forest are buffers.
EU, NATO and euro membership plus low debt support further convergence from an already high consumption level, against severe depopulation, aging, high inequality and recurring political instability.

Security has improved dramatically, but it rests on authoritarian consolidation, alongside a heavy interest burden (14% of revenue), rising water stress and hurricane and drought exposure; remittances and a low base favour modest gains.

World-leading governance and readiness to adapt, a tech and capital hub well placed for superintelligence gains, offset by near-total dependence on imported food and energy, sea-level and heat exposure, and its position in any US-China conflict.

Strong institutions, low debt, a food surplus, wind power and low inequality (which helps the 9-in-10 test for abundance) make Denmark very resilient; sea-level rise and Greenland or Baltic geopolitics are the main risks.

Lebanon is still in a deep financial and state collapse, with maximum water stress, repeated war with Israel and a large refugee load; recovery from today's depressed level makes 'better' reachable, but renewed conflict keeps collapse risk high.

Among the poorest countries judged here (GDP about $2,000 PPP, 37% undernourished, 35% electricity) with high climate vulnerability and weak institutions, though two decades of peace and peaceful handovers of power support gradual gains.
